questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Assess practical design of lifecycle policies, CRD design, and safe cleanup in a multi-tenant cluster. It probes reconciliation logic, finalizers, and observability.

## Key Concepts
- Kubernetes CRD and controller pattern
- TTL-based cleanup, namespace scoping
- Finalizers and safe deletion of dependent resources
- Handling race conditions, backoff, and in-flight work
- Observability: metrics, events, status conditions

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: ttlpolicies.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  versions:
  - name: v1alpha1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              namespaceSelector:
                type: string
              ttlSeconds:
                type: integer
              deleteResources:
                type: boolean
              prunePVCs:
                type: boolean
              finalizers:
                type: array
                items:
                  type: string
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: ttlpolicies
    singular: ttlpolicy
    kind: TTLPolicy
    shortNames: [ ttlpol ]
```

```go
  // manage finalizers and status.conditions
  return ctrl.Result{RequeueAfter: time.Until(nextExpiry)}, nil
}
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests practical understanding of Deployment rollout behavior, readiness/liveness probes, and how to verify zero-downtime during a push.

## Key Concepts

- RollingUpdate strategy
- maxUnavailable and maxSurge semantics
- readinessProbe and livenessProbe configuration
- kubectl rollout status and rollout history for observability

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 2
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0
      maxSurge: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: your-image:tag
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 15
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you validate zero-downtime if the new image has longer startup?
- How would you handle a rollout failure and roll back?

```yaml
kind: Deployment

  name: api

  template:

      containers:
      - name: api

          limits:
```

```yaml
  name: default-mem-limits
  namespace: prod

    defaultRequest:
      memory: "256Mi"
    type: Container
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical familiarity with Kubernetes CronJobs, concurrency control, job history, and log persistence via PVCs.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob scheduling and concurrencyPolicy
- Job history limits and reliability
- Pod security and resource requests/limits
- Logs persistence using a PersistentVolumeClaim
- Verifying runs with kubectl commands

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: db-backup-cron
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 1
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: backup
            image: backup-tool:latest
            args: ["/bin/sh","-c","/backup/backup.sh > /backups/backup-$(date +%F).log"]
            volumeMounts:
            - name: backups
              mountPath: /backups
          volumes:
          - name: backups
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: backup-logs
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "100m"
              memory: "128Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "256Mi"
```

## Why This Is Asked

Tests practical policy enforcement in a real cluster, using Gatekeeper and Rego to codify organizational rules, along with testing and observability considerations.

## Key Concepts

- Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
- Rego-based policy; match blocks on Deployment kinds
- Namespace labeling for multi-tenancy; alerting via Gatekeeper audit events

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8sallowedimages
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sAllowedImages
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8sallowedimages
      violation[{"msg":"image from disallowed registry"}] {
        input.review.object.kind == "Deployment"
        container := input.review.object.spec.template.spec.containers[_]
        not startswith(container.image, "approved-registry/")
      }
```

```yaml
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sAllowedImages
metadata:
  name: stage-allowlist
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
    - apiGroups: ["apps"]
      kinds: ["Deployment"]
  parameters:
    allowedImages:
      - "approved-registry/"
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you test rollback if a legitimate image is blocked due to a policy change?
- What are performance implications of Gatekeeper in a busy cluster, and how would you mitigate them?
